title: Zorn's lemma and Hamel bases
promptMarkdown:
1. Using Zorn's lemma, show that every vector space $V\neq\{0\}$ has a Hamel basis. Be explicit about the partially ordered set, why chains have upper bounds, and why a maximal element spans.
2. In under 120 words, combine this with the result of unit 3 (no countable Hamel basis in an infinite-dimensional Banach space) to explain why Hamel bases are the wrong notion of basis for Banach spaces, and what notion will replace them for Hilbert spaces later in the course.
hintLadder: Take $E$ to be the set of linearly independent subsets of $V$, ordered by inclusion. Why is $E$ nonempty?
For a chain of independent sets, consider the union. A finite dependence among its elements involves finitely many sets of the chain; which one contains them all?
If a maximal independent set $H$ did not span $V$, pick $v\notin\operatorname{span}H$ and consider $H\cup\{v\}$.

criteria.criterion: Independent subsets ordered by inclusion; nonempty.
Union of a chain is independent (finite dependence lives in one member) and is an upper bound.
A maximal independent set spans; otherwise it can be enlarged.
Hamel bases of infinite-dimensional Banach spaces are uncountable and non-constructive; orthonormal (Schauder-type) bases with infinite sums replace them.

difficulty.basis: The lesson sketches the Zorn argument; the exercise asks for it in full (the partial order, upper bounds for chains, why a maximal element spans) and for a short paragraph linking it to unit 3's result on countable bases.
